Consequently F_j/F_(j+1) strictly decreases from infinity to zero: at zero use B∼t; at infinity apply the integral kernels to the integrable positive B by dominated convergence. Positivity gives no crossing if qh≥0, including either one-zero case, and D_j≡0 if q=h=0; otherwise the ratio gives a simple sign crossing from q to h. The phrase 'opposite steady-state loss-weighted source difference' in the introductory prose should be read via the explicit qh<0 and h=bS1−aS2, not as inserting a second minus sign. Integrating before the first zero forces the next zero to be later, and F_(j+1)≤(t/j)F_j implies t_j≥j|q/h|. For u=v=k in the crossing regime, a≠b and both r_-(k) and the rate gap increase. For 0<s<t the quotient B_k(s)/B_k(t) increases strictly, so the inverse kernel-integral ratio falls strictly with k, as does its crossing time. Its fixed-t limit is r/(e^(rt)−1), r=(a+b)/2, by dominated convergence of the kernel quotient; bracketing its strictly decreasing root gives the exact positive limit. value.rationale: The problem distinguishes fast sensor ordering, cumulative exposure ordering, and equilibrium ordering in a motivated compartment model. The exact criterion separates the existence of a reversal from its time, shows why repeated integration postpones the reversal without bound, and establishes a nonzero lower time even for arbitrarily strong symmetric exchange. These give a model benchmark and a limitation on naive extrapolation from early sensor readings, not an empirical building-design prescription or a claim for nonzero initial data or asymmetric mixing changes.
